concepts.title: How a business school might talk about your research.
concepts.one_liner: You have a brand: you, and there are many impressions you want to build up about your brand.
concepts.content: You have a brand: you. There are many impressions you want to build up about your brand: that person always does great work, they have good ideas, they give great talks, they write wonderful software. Promote your brand. Build up a great reputation for yourself by consistently behaving in the way you'd like to be thought of.
concepts.motivation_md: Building a strong personal brand helps establish your reputation and communicates your consistent strengths and qualities to others, which is crucial in academia and business.

- Promote your brand by consistently demonstrating your strengths.
- Building a great reputation requires consistent behavior aligned with how you want to be seen.

concepts.title: Please don't report to me and say, "This instance doesn't work."
concepts.one_liner: Why doesn't it work? Why should it work? Is there a simpler case we can make work?
concepts.content: Why doesn't it work? Why should it work? Is there a simpler case we can make work? Do you think it's a general issue that affects all problems of this category? Can you think of what's not working? Can you contort things to make an example that does work? At the very least, can you make it fail worse, so we understand some aspects of the system?
concepts.motivation_md: When reporting problems, providing detailed analysis and examples helps clarify issues and guides towards solutions, rather than just stating failure.
concepts.recap_md:
- Don't just say "this instance doesn't work" without analysis.
- Ask why it doesn't work and if a simpler case can be solved.
- Try to understand and illustrate the problem more deeply.

concepts.title: Progress.
concepts.one_liner: Progress can include things like "I've shown why this doesn't work," "I've simplified the task to get it to start working," or "I spent the whole time reading because I know I have to understand this before I can make any progress."
concepts.content: I love to hear about progress when I meet with students, but note that I have a very general notion of progress. Progress can include things like "I've shown why this doesn't work," "I've simplified the task to get it to start working," or "I spent the whole time reading because I know I have to understand this before I can make any progress."
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing diverse forms of progress encourages persistence and values understanding and problem refinement as important steps in research.
concepts.recap_md:
- Progress is broadly defined and valued.
- It can mean showing why something doesn't work.
- It can also mean simplifying tasks or gaining understanding through reading.

concepts.title: "Slow down to speed up."
concepts.one_liner: The first piece of advice can go on a bumper sticker: "Slow down to speed up."
concepts.content:
The first piece of advice can go on a bumper sticker: **"Slow down to speed up."** In classes, the world is rigged. There's a simple correct answer and the problem is structured to let you come to that answer. You get feedback with the correct answer within a day after you submit anything.

Research is different. No one tells you the right answer, and we may not know if there is a right answer. We don't know if something doesn't work because there's a silly mistake in the program or because a broad set of assumptions is flawed.

How do you deal with that? Take things slowly. Verify your assumptions. Understand the thing, whatever it is—the program, the algorithm, or the proof. As you do experiments, only change one thing at a time, so you know what the outcome of the experiment means.

It may feel like you're going slowly, but you'll be making much more progress than if you flail around, trying different things, but not understanding what's going on.

(see figure: Research advice for a bumper sticker.)
concepts.motivation_md: Research problems lack clear answers and immediate feedback, so slowing down to verify assumptions and understand each step helps avoid wasted effort and leads to more meaningful progress.
concepts.recap_md:
- "Slow down to speed up" means taking time to understand and verify assumptions in research.
- Change only one thing at a time in experiments to interpret results correctly.
- Progress feels slow but is more effective than flailing without understanding.

concepts.title: Please don't tell me "it doesn't work."
concepts.one_liner: Please don't tell me "it doesn't work."
concepts.content: **Please don't tell me "it doesn't work."** Of course, it doesn't work. If there's a single mistake in the chain, the whole thing won't work, and how could you possibly go through all those steps without making a mistake somewhere? What I want to hear instead is something like, "I've narrowed down the problem to step B. Until step A, you can see that it works because you put in X and you get Y out, as we expect. You can see how it fails here at B. I've ruled out W and Z as the cause."
concepts.motivation_md: Instead of vague failure reports, detailed diagnostics help isolate where and why a problem occurs, facilitating effective debugging and progress.
concepts.recap_md:
- Saying "it doesn't work" is unhelpful without specifics.
- Narrow down the problem to a particular step.
- Explain what works before the failure and what has been ruled out as causes.

concepts.title: "This sounds like hard work."
concepts.content:
**"This sounds like hard work."** Yes. It's no longer about being smart. By now, everyone around you is smart. In graduate school, it's the **hard workers** who pull ahead. This happens in sports, too. You always read stories about how hard the great players work, being the first ones out to practice, the last ones to leave, and so on.

A co-author, who generally works harder than I do, tells me I should add comments here about the importance of taking time off from work and maintaining a good life/work balance. That is true: you should work at a pace you can sustain, and you should refresh yourself by making time for the things that matter more than work, such as relationships, service, and relaxation. Perhaps the point is to protect your time so you will have enough time to do the research well.
concepts.motivation_md: Success depends more on sustained hard work than innate intelligence, balanced with rest and life priorities to maintain long-term productivity.
concepts.recap_md:
- Hard work, not just intelligence, drives success in graduate school.
- Great achievers often work harder and longer than others.
- Maintaining work-life balance is important for sustainable research.

concepts.title: "How do I get myself to work hard enough to do research well?"
concepts.one_liner: "How do I get myself to work hard enough to do research well?"
concepts.content: **"How do I get myself to work hard enough to do research well?"** It all plays out if you love what you're doing. You become good at it because you spend time at it and you do that because you enjoy it. So pick something to work on that you can love. If you're not the type who falls in love with a problem, then just know that working hard is what you have to do to succeed at research.
concepts.motivation_md: Loving your research motivates sustained effort and skill development; without passion, hard work remains essential for success.
concepts.recap_md:
- Loving your work helps you work hard and improve.
- Choose research problems you can be passionate about.
- If not passionate, recognize that hard work is still necessary.

concepts.title: The above isn't completely true.
concepts.one_liner: Beyond working hard, there's also steering.
concepts.content: **The above isn't completely true.** Beyond working hard, there's also **steering**. We're like boats. We need motors—that's the part about working hard. But we also need a rudder for steering—that means stepping back periodically to make sure we're working on the right thing. On the topic of steering, I find time management books to be very helpful. They teach you how to spend your time solving the right problems.
concepts.motivation_md: Hard work alone isn't enough; periodically reassessing direction ensures effort is focused on the right problems, improving research effectiveness.
concepts.recap_md:
- Working hard is like having a motor.
- Steering means stepping back to check if you're on the right path.
- Time management helps focus on solving the right problems.

concepts.title: Strategies for success.
concepts.content:
**Strategies for success.** Here is a parable, as told by my friend Yair Weiss. There is a weak and a strong graduate student. They are both asked by their advisor to try a particular approach to solving a research problem. The weak student does exactly what the advisor has asked. But the advisor's solution fails, and the student reports that failure. The strong student starts doing what the advisor has asked, sees that it doesn't work, looks around within some epsilon ball of the original proposal to find what does work, and reports that solution.

(see figure: The parable of the two students.)
concepts.motivation_md: Success in research involves adapting and exploring beyond initial instructions to find workable solutions rather than just reporting failures.
concepts.recap_md:
- The weak student follows instructions exactly and reports failure.
- The strong student explores nearby alternatives to find success.
- Adaptation and initiative lead to better research outcomes.

concepts.title: Sometimes it's useful to think that everyone else is completely off-track.
concepts.one_liner: Sometimes it's useful to think that everyone else is completely off-track.
concepts.content: **Sometimes it's useful to think that everyone else is completely off-track.** This lets you do things that no one else is doing. It's best not to be too vocal about that. You can say something like, "Oh, I just thought I'd try out this direction."
concepts.motivation_md: Believing others are off-track encourages exploring unique directions, fostering innovation while maintaining diplomacy in communication.
concepts.recap_md:
- Thinking others are off-track can open unique research paths.
- This mindset encourages doing what no one else is doing.
- Be discreet when expressing unconventional ideas.

concepts.title: It's also sometimes useful to remember
concepts.one_liner: It's also sometimes useful to remember that many smart people have worked on this and related problems.
concepts.content: **It's also sometimes useful to remember** that many smart people have worked on this and related problems and written their thoughts and results down in papers. Don't be caught flat-footed with a large body of closely related literature that you aren't familiar with.
concepts.motivation_md: Being aware of existing literature prevents redundant work and informs your research with prior insights and results.
concepts.recap_md:
- Many smart people have studied related problems.
- Their work is documented in papers.
- Familiarize yourself with related literature to avoid being unprepared.
